questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Sequences / Arithmetic sequences and their sums
questions.stem: The sequence $3,\ 10,\ 17,\ 24,\ \ldots$ is arithmetic. Its common difference $d$ is
questions.solution:
The common difference is what each term adds to the one before it.

Subtract a neighbouring pair:
$$d=10-3=7.$$

The same gap appears further along: $17-10=7$ and $24-17=7$. A constant gap is what makes the list arithmetic, so $d=7$.
distractorRationale: $3$ is the opening term $a_1$. The gap between terms is a subtraction, not the first entry.
Correct. Neighbouring terms differ by $7$, since $10-3=17-10=24-17=7$.
$10$ is the second term, copied out without subtracting the term before it.
Skipped over a term and used $17-3$, which spans two gaps rather than one.

questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Sequences / Arithmetic sequences and their sums
questions.stem: An arithmetic sequence has $a_1=-5$ and $d=6$. Find $a_{12}$.
questions.solution:
Every step forward adds $d$. Travelling from $a_1$ out to $a_{12}$ takes $12-1=11$ steps, because the first term is where the counting starts rather than a step in its own right.
$$a_{12}=a_1+11d=-5+11 \times 6=-5+66=61.$$
distractorRationale: Correct. Eleven steps of $6$ added to $-5$ give $-5+66=61$.
Reported $11d$ on its own and never added the starting value $-5$.
Took $12$ steps rather than $11$, computing $-5+12 \times 6$.
Sign slip on the starting value: added $+5$ to $66$ instead of $-5$.

questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Sequences / Arithmetic sequences and their sums
questions.stem: An arithmetic sequence has $a_3=11$ and $a_7=27$. Find $S_{10}$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — the common difference.** Four steps separate $a_3$ from $a_7$, so
$$d=\frac{27-11}{7-3}=\frac{16}{4}=4.$$

**Step 2 — the opening term.** Walk two steps back from $a_3$:
$$a_1=11-2 \times 4=3.$$

**Step 3 — add up ten terms.** Ten terms enclose nine steps, so the bracket carries $9d$:
$$S_{10}=\frac{10}{2}\bigl(2 \times 3+9 \times 4\bigr)=5 \times 42=210.$$
distractorRationale: Added only nine terms. This is $S_9$, and the tenth term $39$ is missing from it.
Divided by $5$ instead of $4$ when finding $d$, counting terms where gaps were wanted. That yields $d=3.2$ and a starting value of $4.6$.
Wrote $2a_1+10d$ inside the bracket, using ten steps where nine belong.

questions.stem: The five interior angles of a convex pentagon total $540^\circ$ and form an arithmetic sequence of common difference $20^\circ$. The largest angle is
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — the middle angle.** When an arithmetic list has an odd length, its middle entry equals the mean of the whole list. Five angles totalling $540^\circ$ therefore give
$$a_3=\frac{540^\circ}{5}=108^\circ.$$

**Step 2 — climb to the top.** The biggest angle is $a_5$, which sits two steps above the middle:
$$a_5=108^\circ+2 \times 20^\circ=148^\circ.$$

The five angles run $68^\circ,\ 88^\circ,\ 108^\circ,\ 128^\circ,\ 148^\circ$, and they do total $540^\circ$.
distractorRationale: This is $a_2$. Counting downwards from the middle reaches the small angles, not the large ones.
This is the mean angle $a_3$. A mean sits in the middle of the list, so it cannot be the largest entry.
Climbed one step of $20^\circ$ above the middle instead of two, landing on $a_4$.
Correct. The middle angle is $108^\circ$ and the largest lies two steps above it: $108^\circ+40^\circ=148^\circ$.

questions.subject: math
questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Sequences / Geometric sequences and their sums
questions.stem: A geometric sequence has $a_1=3$ and common ratio $q=2$. Find $a_6$.
questions.solution:
The ratio is applied once per step, and reaching $a_6$ from $a_1$ takes five steps.
$$a_6=a_1q^{5}=3 \times 2^{5}=3 \times 32=96.$$
distractorRationale: Used $q^{4}$, one step short of the sixth term.
Computed $2^{6}$ and never multiplied by the starting value $3$.
Correct. Five doublings applied to $3$ give $3 \times 32=96$.
Used $q^{6}$, as if six steps separated the first term from the sixth.

questions.stem: A geometric sequence has $a_1=2$ and $q=3$. Find $S_5$.
questions.solution:
Because $q \neq 1$, five terms add to
$$S_5=\frac{a_1(q^{5}-1)}{q-1}=\frac{2(243-1)}{3-1}=\frac{484}{2}=242.$$

Writing the terms out confirms it: $2,\ 6,\ 18,\ 54,\ 162$ add to $242$.
distractorRationale: Dropped the factor $a_1$ and evaluated $\dfrac{3^{5}-1}{3-1}$ alone.
This is $a_5=2 \times 81$, the last term rather than the running total.
Began adding at $a_2$, so the opening term $2$ never entered the total.

questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Sequences / Geometric sequences and their sums
questions.stem: In a geometric sequence of positive terms, $a_2=6$ and $a_4=54$. Find $q$.
questions.solution:
Two steps separate $a_2$ from $a_4$, so the ratio acts twice:
$$\frac{a_4}{a_2}=q^{2}=\frac{54}{6}=9.$$

A square root gives $q=3$ or $q=-3$. Every term is positive, and a negative ratio would flip the sign at each step, so
$$q=3.$$
distractorRationale: Correct. $q^{2}=9$, and positive terms rule out $q=-3$, leaving $q=3$.
Stopped at $q^{2}=9$ without taking the square root.
Treated the list as arithmetic and reported $\dfrac{54-6}{2}=24$ as a common difference.
Subtracted where a division was needed, giving $54-6$.

questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Sequences / Geometric sequences and their sums
questions.stem: A geometric sequence of real numbers has $a_1=4$ and $a_3=36$. Find $a_5$.
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — the ratio, with two cases.** Two steps give
$$q^{2}=\frac{36}{4}=9,$$
so $q=3$ or $q=-3$. Nothing in the question rules either out, so both have to be carried.

**Step 2 — the two cases agree.** Four steps separate $a_1$ from $a_5$, and
$$q^{4}=(q^{2})^{2}=81$$
whatever sign $q$ carries, because the square erases it. So
$$a_5=4 \times 81=324$$
in both cases, and the ambiguity never reaches the answer.
distractorRationale: Read the list as arithmetic, taking $\dfrac{36-4}{2}=16$ as a common difference and then $4+4 \times 16$.
Advanced one step past $a_3$ instead of two, computing $36 \times 3$.
Correct. $q^{2}=9$ forces $q^{4}=81$ for either sign, so $a_5=4 \times 81=324$.
Squared $a_3$ without dividing by $a_1$. The relation is $a_5=\dfrac{a_3^{2}}{a_1}$.

questions.stem: A sequence is given by $a_n=5n-2$. Find $a_4$.
distractorRationale: Substituted $n=3$, which returns the term before the one asked for.
Correct. $5 \times 4=20$, and $20-2=18$.
Stopped at $5 \times 4$ and never subtracted the $2$.
Sign slip: added the $2$ where the rule subtracts it.

questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Sequences / General terms, recurrences and S(n) relations
questions.stem: The list $4,\ 7,\ 10,\ 13,\ \ldots$ carries on with the same pattern. Its general term is
questions.solution:
Neighbouring entries rise by $3$ every time, so this is arithmetic with $d=3$ starting from $a_1=4$.

Substitute into $a_n=a_1+(n-1)d$ and expand:
$$a_n=4+3(n-1)=3n+1.$$

Testing the rule: it returns $4$, then $7$, then $10$, which is the list given.
distractorRationale: Correct. $4+3(n-1)$ expands to $3n+1$, which reproduces $4,\ 7,\ 10,\ 13$ in turn.
Expanded $4+3(n-1)$ as $3n-1$, subtracting the $3$ from nothing instead of from $4$.
Multiplied the opening term by $n$. That rule delivers $4,\ 8,\ 12$, a different list.
Put the common difference in the constant slot, so the terms climb by $1$ per step rather than by $3$.

questions.syllabusRef: M-2 / Functions and Sequences / Sequences / General terms, recurrences and S(n) relations
questions.stem: A sequence $\{a_n\}$ has running total $S_n=n^{2}+4n$ for every $n \ge 1$. Then $a_n$ equals
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — subtract consecutive totals.** For $n \ge 2$, the $n$th entry is whatever the running total gains at step $n$:
$$a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}.$$

Expanding the earlier total,
$$(n-1)^{2}+4(n-1)=n^{2}+2n-3,$$
so the gain is
$$a_n=(n^{2}+4n)-(n^{2}+2n-3)=2n+3.$$

**Step 2 — treat the opening term separately.** Subtraction says nothing about $a_1$, which has to come from $S_1=1+4=5$. The formula returns $2+3=5$ as well, so a single rule covers every index.
distractorRationale: Reported $S_n$ itself. A running total is not an individual entry unless only one entry has been added.
Correct. $S_n-S_{n-1}=2n+3$, and that rule also delivers $a_1=5=S_1$.
Divided $S_n$ by $n$, which produces the average of the first $n$ entries rather than the $n$th one.
Computed $S_{n+1}-S_n$, shifting the index by one and returning the next entry instead.
